title: Upholstery fabric identification and colourfastness
audience: Upholstery cleaners who identify fabrics and test colourfastness before treatment.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: Safe Work Australia, Hazardous chemicals register (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, Understanding safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals (no date shown in the text read); WorkSafe Victoria, The hierarchy of control (reviewed 30 July 2022). No Australian upholstery cleaning standard has been confirmed.
learningOutcomes: Identify the common upholstery fabrics and their sensitivity to water and products.
Carry out a colourfastness check before a treatment.
Refuse a treatment where the fabric or colour is not suitable.

instruction.heading: Common upholstery fabrics
instruction.body: Upholstery covers are made from many materials, and each responds differently to water, heat, brushing and product. Cotton and linen are cellulose fibres; they can shrink and some of their dyes can run when they are wet. Wool is a protein fibre and is treated with more care. Synthetic blends and microfibre are common in modern furniture; microfibre is a fine fibre that can hold soil in its surface and can be marked by friction. Velvet, chenille and other pile fabrics have a direction, and a pile can crush or mark under hard brushing. Leather is a natural hide with a finish, and it is not treated like a textile. Vinyl and polyurethane coatings are a surface layer over a backing, and some solvents can damage that layer. The label, the feel and the pile are the first clues, and no single clue is conclusive.

instruction.heading: Identifying the fabric on the job
instruction.body: Read the manufacturer's care label first, where one is present, and record it exactly as written. Then look at the fabric in good light with a magnifier. Look at the weave or knit, the pile and its direction, the sheen and the surface finish. Feel the fabric, and check the back and any hidden seam allowance for the backing and the construction. Where the fabric cannot be identified with confidence, record it as unidentified and treat it as sensitive, with the most conservative method and a test before any main treatment. Do not guess the material from the colour or the price of the furniture.

instruction.heading: The colourfastness check
instruction.body: Test colourfastness on an inconspicuous area, such as the underside of a cushion, a hidden seam or the back of a panel. Use the planned product at the planned dilution. Apply a small amount to a white test cloth and press it gently onto the test area, rather than rubbing it. Check the cloth for colour transfer, and check the test area for any change in shade or any damage. Compare the cloth with a blank white cloth held in the same light, because a faint mark is easier to judge that way. Repeat the test on a second colour or a second fabric panel if the item has more than one. Allow the test area to dry fully before the result is judged, and record the time and the result.

instruction.heading: Reading a failed result
instruction.body: A colour transfer onto the white cloth means the product is not suitable for that fabric and colour, and the fabric is not treated with that product. Do not try a stronger version of the same product, and do not switch to a product that the test has not been run on. Look also for shrinkage, stiffness, pile crush and cracking or lifting of a coating. Any of these results is a reason to refuse the treatment or to choose a gentler approach. Record the test, the result and the decision, and tell the customer what was found and what the next option is.

instruction.heading: Pile fabrics and gentle handling
instruction.body: Pile fabrics need a gentle method. Work with the direction of the pile, using a soft brush rather than a stiff one, and avoid hard brushing in all directions, because it can flatten the pile, mark the surface or lift the nap. Test the method on an inconspicuous area before the main treatment, and check the result after drying in the same light. A pile that has been crushed may not recover, so record its condition before the work starts, and tell the customer if a change is likely.

instruction.heading: Leather and vinyl are not fabric
instruction.body: Leather and vinyl are not treated like fabric. Leather has a finish over a natural hide, and the finish can be damaged by products that work well on textiles. Vinyl and polyurethane have a coating over a backing, and the coating can be softened, marked or lifted by some solvents. Identify the material first, check the label, and test the approach on an inconspicuous area. Where the material is unclear, or the finish is already cracking or peeling, refer the item for a specialist assessment rather than treating it as fabric.

instruction.heading: Refusing treatments and offering alternatives
instruction.body: Refuse a treatment where the colour transfers, the fabric shrinks, the pile is damaged or the coating reacts in the test. Offer a conservative alternative that has been tested, or refer the item for a specialist assessment. Explain the limit to the customer, and do not promise that a stain will come out of a fabric that has failed the test. Record the test, the result, the decision, the alternative offered and the customer's response.

procedure: Read and record the care label where present, and identify the fabric from its feel, weave or knit and pile.
Identify whether the item is fabric, leather or vinyl, and treat any unidentified material as sensitive.
Test colourfastness on an inconspicuous area with the planned product and dilution, by pressing a white cloth gently onto the area.
Compare the cloth with a blank cloth in the same light, check the test area for shade change, shrinkage, pile damage or coating reaction, and allow it to dry fully.
Refuse any treatment that fails the test, do not use a stronger product, and offer a tested conservative alternative or a referral.
Record the fabric, the label, the test, the result, the decision and the customer's response.

workedExamples.situation: A velvet armchair shows colour transfer onto a white cloth during the colourfastness test on the underside of a cushion.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do with the planned product, and what do you offer the customer?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not treat the armchair with the planned product. Record the transfer, the test area and the product, and photograph the cloth and the test area with permission. Do not brush the velvet hard to lift the stain. Offer a conservative approach that has been tested on the same cushion underside, and explain that the stain may not fully come out. If the customer wants more, refer the item for a specialist assessment, and record the referral and the customer's response.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A cotton slipcover shows a coloured dye line along a hidden seam when the test is carried out on the inside hem. The customer asks for a full wet clean of the cover so it will match the rest of the room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is a full wet clean acceptable, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not on the strength of this test. The dye line shows that the colour may move when wet, so a full wet clean is refused. Record the test on the hem, the dye line and the product used. Offer a lower-moisture approach that has been tested, or suggest that the cover is removed and cleaned as the maker directs, and record that as the customer's choice. Explain the limit before any work starts.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A vinyl dining chair has a sticky surface and an unknown finish. The customer asks for a solvent to remove the marks quickly.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you use a solvent, and what do you check first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use a solvent on an unidentified vinyl or coated finish. Identify the material from the label or the supplier, and test the planned approach on an inconspicuous area, such as under the seat. Record the finish condition and the result of the test. If the finish reacts, or the material cannot be identified, refuse the solvent and refer the chair for a specialist assessment, and record the reasons.

equipmentAndPpe: White test cloth, and a blank white cloth for comparison
Approved upholstery products, each with its label and a current safety data sheet
Soft brush suited to pile fabric, and no stiff brush for pile
Magnifier and torch for identifying the weave, knit and pile
Gloves and eye protection, as set by the product's safety data sheet
Test record sheet and camera or phone, used only with permission

commonErrors.error: Skipping the colourfastness check on a plain fabric.
commonErrors.prevention: Test every item before treatment, including plain and familiar fabrics.

commonErrors.error: Brushing velvet or other pile hard to lift a stain.
commonErrors.prevention: Work with the pile direction, use a soft brush, and test the method first.

commonErrors.error: Treating leather or vinyl as fabric.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the material first, and refer any unclear or failing finish.

commonErrors.error: Using a stronger product after a failed test.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the result, and offer only a tested alternative or a referral.

commonErrors.error: Guessing the fabric from its colour or from the price of the furniture.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the label, the feel, the weave and the pile, and treat any unidentified fabric as sensitive.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Each hazardous chemical on the workplace register is matched to a current safety data sheet, and the register is kept where workers can reach it (Safe Work Australia, Hazardous chemicals register, fetched 2026-11-03; no date shown).

A safety data sheet has 16 headings, and the supplier can provide a copy at no cost on request. It should have been prepared within the last five years (Safe Work Australia, Understanding safety data sheets, fetched 2026-11-03).
The hierarchy of control places personal protective equipment last, as the weakest option (WorkSafe Victoria, reviewed 30/07/2022).
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.
The test method in this lesson is general practice.

qualityStandard: The fabric is identified, or recorded as unidentified and treated as sensitive, before treatment in the practical.
The colourfastness test is completed on an inconspicuous area with the planned product, and read after drying, in the practical.
A colour transfer is correctly identified and the treatment refused in the case study.
A pile fabric is treated with a gentle method, and no hard brushing is used, in the case study.
documentationEvidence: Fabric identification record, with the label exactly as written where present
Colourfastness record with the product, dilution, area, time, drying time and result
Refusal and referral record, with the alternative offered and the customer's response
Photographs of the test area and the white cloth, taken with permission
summary: Identify the fabric, or record it as unidentified, before any treatment.
Test colourfastness on an inconspicuous area with the planned product, and judge the result after drying.
Use a gentle, pile-aware method, and treat leather and vinyl as different materials.
Refuse treatments that fail the test, and record the decision and the alternative.

knowledgeChecks.question: How is colourfastness tested?
options: By looking at the fabric closely in good light and deciding that it is fine for the job at hand
By smelling the product to check that it is safe for the fabric and the owner and the room today
Apply a small amount of the planned product to a white cloth on an inconspicuous area and check for transfer

knowledgeChecks.question: Colour transfers onto the white cloth. What is correct?
options: Refuse that product and offer a tested conservative approach or a referral
Treat the whole item with the product, since the test was done on a small spot
Mix in a stronger product to improve the result on the stain area

knowledgeChecks.question: Why treat leather and vinyl differently from fabric?
options: They look the same, so the method is the same for each type of surface in the room
They are not textiles, and their finishes or coatings can react to products that suit fabric
They are cheaper to buy, so less care is needed when cleaning them on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: A velvet fabric needs cleaning. What is the safe approach?
options: Brush hard in all directions to lift the stain out of the pile fast
Use a gentle, pile-aware method after a test on an inconspicuous area
Scrub with a stiff brush and a strong product to lift the stain
